Less frequent gas- tric neoplasms include lymphomas (see MALT lym- phoma, above) and carcinoid tumours (see above). Dietary factors, such as high consumption of salted or smoked foods, are thought to play a role in the develop- ment of gastric cancer. Helicobacter pylori infection, and resultant gastritis, plays a role in gastric lympho- mas, and may also be a factor in gastric cancer. Howev- er, it is not yet clear if elimination of Helicobacter py- lori infection will prove useful in preventing the development of gastric cancer.2,3 Early disease is relatively asymptomatic or produces non- specific gastrointestinal symptoms such as dyspepsia. There is concern that the use of antisecretory drugs for these symptoms may delay the diagnosis of gastric cancer (see Gastric Carcinoma, under Omeprazole Precautions, p.1754). Gastric epithelial dysplasia is a premalignant con- dition, and warrants follow-up and possible surgical inter- vention. Similarly, persistent gastric ulcers may be malig- nant. More advanced disease, which is the norm at presentation in most western countries, may produce dis- comfort or pain, anaemia, weight loss, and anorexia; ob- struction, haemorrhage, and perforation may develop. Ex- tension to the liver and pancreas, and lymphatic and blood- borne (portal) metastases may occur. Surgery is the mainstay of treatment for locoregional dis- ease.4,5 There is some uncertainty, however, about the ap- propriate extent of surgery and associated lymph-node dis- section.1,5,6 Typical 5-year survival rates in western patients have ranged from about 50 to 80% in those with stage I disease to 13% in those with stage III;6,7 although much higher survival rates (over 96% in stage I disease and nearly 45% in stage III) have been reported in Japan,6 Japanese and western patients may not be equivalent, a fact that has made comparisons difficult.
